descripcion: At C1 the preposition stops being a piece of accuracy to get right and becomes a piece of meaning to choose. A cluster of verbs takes more than one preposition, each with a distinct sense — *consist of* lists parts while *consist in* identifies an essence, *concerned with* names a subject while *concerned about* admits a worry — so the wrong preposition here does not read as a learner error but as a different and unintended claim. Alongside this sits a register decision: stranding the preposition is neutral, fronting it (*the premise on which the argument rests*) is formal written English, and a C1 writer chooses deliberately between them rather than defaulting to one.

cuadroReferencia.titulo: Verbs where the preposition changes the meaning
filas: *of* lists the parts; *in* identifies the essence
*with* a person; *to* a proposal; *on* a joint decision
*with* names the subject matter; *about* admits a worry
*in* points forward to the effect; *from* points back to the cause
*with* an offence; *for* a sum of money
*for* replaces the original; *with* names the replacement
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: In each pair both options are correct English — only one is the claim you meant.

ejemplos.texto: The committee consists of nine members; the difficulty consists in getting them to agree.
The paper is concerned with migration patterns, not concerned about them.
They agreed with us on the diagnosis but never agreed to the proposal.
The premise on which the whole argument rests is never stated.
That's the premise the whole argument rests on.
The shortfall resulted from a forecasting error and resulted in a hiring freeze.

notas: Where a verb takes two prepositions, treat the choice as semantic rather than idiomatic: the reader will take the meaning the preposition signals, not the one you intended.

Fronting the preposition raises the register noticeably and works best once or twice in a piece; using it throughout reads as stiff rather than educated, and stranding remains correct at every level of formality.
*Compare to* and *compare with* have largely merged in current usage, but the distinction still carries in careful academic prose, so keep it where precision matters.

Nominalising a prepositional verb usually changes the preposition too: *depend on* becomes *dependence on*, but *result in* becomes *the result of*. The noun's preposition has to be checked separately.

contraste.es: Spanish resolves several of these distinctions lexically rather than through the preposition: consist of and consist in are both consistir en, so the distinction has no Spanish trigger to carry it and has to be learned as new information rather than mapped. The register axis is also missing, because Spanish must front the preposition in every register — meaning a Spanish speaker at C1 has no native instinct for when fronting sounds formal, and either avoids it entirely or applies it uniformly.
contraste.de: German has an exact parallel for one key pair: bestehen aus (consist of) and bestehen in (consist in). Prepositional verbs are just as fixed in German, but the prepositions rarely match (depend on – abhängen von). The register axis is new: German always puts the preposition before the relative pronoun (die Kollegin, mit der ich arbeite), so German speakers have no instinct for when stranding (who I work with) sounds natural and fronting sounds formal.
contraste.it: Italian expresses both consist of and consist in with consistere in, so the distinction has to be learned from scratch. Like Spanish, Italian always places the preposition before the relative pronoun (la collega con cui lavoro), so the register contrast between who I work with and with whom I work has no Italian model.
contraste.fr: French has a useful parallel: consister en (to be made of) against consister à + infinitive (the essence is doing), which maps well onto consist of and consist in. As in the other Romance languages, the preposition always precedes the relative pronoun (avec qui je travaille), so preposition stranding and its register value are new.
contraste.pt: Portuguese uses consistir em for both consist of and consist in, and always places the preposition before the relative pronoun. In colloquial Brazilian Portuguese the preposition is often dropped altogether (a pessoa que eu falei), which can lead to the person I talked instead of the person I talked to.

errores: *The book consists in three parts* — parts take *of*; *in* is reserved for an essence or a difficulty.
Using *concerned about* where *concerned with* is meant, which turns a statement of scope into an expression of anxiety.
Reversing *result in* and *result from*, which inverts the causal direction of the claim.
*They agreed to us* — *to* takes a proposal, not a person: *agreed with us*.
Fronting the preposition in every relative clause, which produces uniformly stiff prose instead of a controlled formal register.
Carrying the verb's preposition over to its nominalisation without checking: *the result in* instead of *the result of*.

redemittel.funcion: keeps the replaced item in focus

autochequeo: For every verb that takes two prepositions, did I choose the one that matches the claim I meant?
Did I check *consist of* against *consist in*, and *concerned with* against *concerned about*?
Are *result in* and *result from* pointing in the right causal direction throughout?
Did I front a preposition only once or twice for effect, rather than in every relative clause?
For each nominalisation, did I verify the noun's preposition instead of reusing the verb's?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on dependent prepositions and what they do to my meaning. (1) For each verb taking more than one preposition, tell me whether the one I chose matches the claim the sentence appears to be making. (2) Check the causal direction of every *result in* and *result from*. (3) Comment on my fronted versus stranded prepositions as a register choice, and say where the register is inconsistent. (4) Check the preposition of any nominalisation. Do not rewrite the text — identify the choices so I can judge them myself.

de: *consist out of* from *bestehen aus* instead of *consist of*.
*wait on* from *warten auf* instead of *wait for*.
it: *depend from* from *dipendere da* instead of *depend on*.
fr: *participate to* from *participer à* instead of *participate in*.
pt: *married with* from *casado com* instead of *married to*.
